specs.anchorText: This section begins the repair, and the tool is almost embarrassingly simple: take a second photograph from somewhere else.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a friendly cartoon robot stands in front of a small 3D scene (a little tree and a ball). On the left, the robot covers one camera-eye with a hand and looks puzzled; the world in its thought bubble appears as a completely flat paper cut-out with no depth. On the right, the same cheerful robot uncovers both camera-eyes, and the thought bubble now shows the same tree and ball as rounded, three-dimensional objects, with two faint dotted sight-lines from its two eyes crossing at the ball to show depth being recovered. Gentle, approachable, like an XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook figure. Soft oranges, blues and greens, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor: one eye makes the world flat, two eyes hand the third dimension back.
specs.alt: A friendly robot covers one camera-eye and imagines a flat paper world, then opens both camera-eyes and imagines the same scene as rounded 3D objects, with two dotted sight-lines crossing at a point, illustrating how a second view restores the depth that a single image destroys.
specs.caption: Close one eye and the world goes politely flat; open both, and the geometry quietly hands the third dimension back.

specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a friendly cartoon detective robot holds a single glowing point in its left hand (representing a pixel in the left photo). In front of it stands a large second photograph shown as a grid of many identical little face-icons (the candidate matches). A bright confident beam from the robot sweeps across that grid and lights up just one thin horizontal stripe of icons, while all the icons off the stripe fade to grey and look relieved-but-dismissed. The lit stripe clearly contains far fewer candidates than the whole grid. Energy of the scene: calm, satisfied, clever. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft blues, purples and warm accents, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: a point in one image confines its match in the other to a single line, turning a 2D search into a 1D one.
specs.alt: A detective robot holding one glowing pixel projects a beam onto a grid of identical candidate matches in a second image, lighting only a single thin horizontal stripe while the rest grey out, showing how the epipolar line collapses correspondence from a full 2D search to a narrow 1D one.
specs.caption: The epipolar line cannot tell you exactly where your match is, only the one line it is hiding on, which already shrinks a million suspects to a thousand.

specs.anchorText: The essential matrix was built as $E = [\mathbf{t}]_\times R$, so it should be possible to take it apart again.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a tiny, dapper cartoon character shaped like a small 3-by-3 grid of glowing cells (a friendly matrix), wearing a little bow tie, stands proudly in the center. From a zipped pocket on its chest it is pulling out two physical objects on a ribbon: a curved rotation arrow (a circular turning arrow) and a straight translation arrow pointing sideways, as if unpacking the hidden relationship between two cameras. Two small friendly cartoon cameras stand on either side, watching as the little matrix reveals how they are posed relative to each other. Gentle, witty, proud expression. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft teal and amber palette, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: a single small matrix secretly carries the rotation and translation between two views and can be unpacked into them.
specs.alt: A small bow-tied character shaped like a glowing three-by-three grid pulls a curved rotation arrow and a straight translation arrow out of its pocket while two cartoon cameras watch, illustrating how the essential matrix packs the relative rotation and translation of two cameras into one tiny object that can be decomposed.
specs.caption: Nine numbers, rank two, and the entire relationship between two photographs is its business; unpack it and out fall the rotation and translation you never measured.

specs.anchorText: Every homography failure in the wild is the same failure: the capture violated one of the two roads of subsection 1.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background, split into two gentle halves. Left half (happy): a cheerful cartoon character with a flat-iron-shaped head smooths two overlapping photographs of a flat distant mountain range into one seamless wide panorama, everything lining up perfectly, a proud smile. Right half (oops): the same character tries the same trick on a close-up scene with a near object (a person waving an arm) in front of distant background; the seam produces a comical ghost, showing the waving arm duplicated and split at the seam, and the character looks sheepish. The contrast between the two halves is the whole point. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft warm palette, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: a homography stitches flat or far scenes flawlessly but ghosts when near and far objects move differently (parallax).
specs.alt: A flat-headed character seamlessly stitches two photos of a distant flat mountain into one panorama on the left, but on the right the same trick on a near waving person produces a ghosted, duplicated arm at the seam, illustrating that a homography works for flat or distant scenes and fails when parallax appears.
specs.caption: A homography assumes the world is flat or you never moved; honor that and panoramas look great, violate it with a near subject and arms get amputated at the seam.

specs.anchorText: The simplest dense matcher is block matching:
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: two cartoon photographs hang side by side, perfectly leveled so their horizontal rows align (a railing-track runs straight across both at the same height to emphasize the row alignment). A friendly little cartoon worker robot holds a small square stamp-shaped patch cut from the left image and slides it left-to-right along the matching straight row of the right image, pausing to compare, with a tiny magnifier checking the fit. A small happy 'snap' sparkle marks where the patch clicks into its best match; a measuring arrow between the left position and the matched position suggests the horizontal shift. The robot looks focused and content. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft greens and blues with warm accents, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: on a rectified pair, matching is just sliding a window along a straight horizontal row to find each pixel's partner, and the column shift is the disparity.
specs.alt: A worker robot slides a small square patch from the left photo along the aligned horizontal row of the right photo until it snaps into its best match, with an arrow marking the horizontal shift, illustrating block matching on a rectified stereo pair where disparity is the column offset of the best match.
specs.caption: Straighten the epipolar lines into rows first, and dense stereo becomes one patient horizontal slide; the column shift where the patch clicks is the disparity.

specs.anchorText: The same quarter-pixel of matcher noise spans two orders of magnitude in metric damage
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a single friendly cartoon stereo-camera character with two lens-eyes measures three objects placed at increasing distance along a receding ground line. The near object (about an arm's length) is being measured with a crisp, confident ruler and a tight checkmark, the character looking like a proud precision instrument. The middle object is measured with a slightly fuzzy ruler and a thoughtful 'maybe' shrug. The far object is barely measurable, shown with a wildly stretched, wobbly rubber ruler and the character wearing a tiny fortune-teller hat and squinting at a crystal ball, comically guessing. The growing fuzziness from near to far is the whole point. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft warm palette, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: the same small disparity error gives tiny depth error up close and huge depth error far away (error grows with the square of distance).
specs.alt: A stereo-camera character measures a near object with a crisp confident ruler, a mid-distance object with a fuzzy ruler and a shrug, and a far object with a wildly stretched wobbly ruler while wearing a fortune-teller hat, illustrating how stereo depth error grows with the square of distance even for the same disparity noise.
specs.caption: At one meter a stereo rig is a precision instrument and at fifty meters it is astrology with a lens cap; depth error grows with the square of distance.

specs.anchorText: two lines in 3D, unlike two lines in a plane, generically do not intersect at all
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: two friendly cartoon arrow-rays, each set out from its own little cartoon camera, are supposed to meet at a single glowing scene point but comically just miss each other, passing slightly above and below with surprised, embarrassed expressions, a tiny gap between them. A gentle dashed bracket marks the small closest-approach gap, and a kindly cartoon referee labeled by a tiny scale-balance icon stands between them placing a marker at the midpoint of the gap, deciding where their meeting 'really' was. Off to the side, a faint comparison hints at two rays meeting at a wide angle (compact, tidy) versus a shallow angle (a long stretched smear), to suggest the sliver problem. Light-hearted, never mean. XKCD-meets-Kurzgesagt textbook style, soft warm palette, generous margins, minimal clutter. No text or lettering in the image. One clear visual metaphor: noisy back-projected rays never truly intersect, so triangulation must define the best non-intersection, and a shallow parallax angle makes that estimate dangerously uncertain.
specs.alt: Two arrow-rays from two cartoon cameras just miss each other near a glowing scene point with a small dashed closest-approach gap, while a referee with a scale icon marks the midpoint, and a side hint contrasts a wide-angle compact crossing with a shallow-angle stretched smear, illustrating why noisy rays never intersect and why small parallax angles ruin triangulation precision.
specs.caption: Two noisy rays were supposed to meet at the point and miss by half a millimeter forever, so a least-squares solver decides where the match really lived; the shallower the angle, the wilder its guess.
